state.misconception_label: Confuses rest and movement on a distance time graph

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This graph shows how far Fido the dog is from his home. What might the negative-sloping section represent? ![A graph with time (secs) on the horizontal axis and distance (m) on the vertical axis. The graph starts at the origin, travels in a straight line up and right, travels horizontally, then travels in a straight line down and right back to the x-axis. ](). I got Fido has fallen asleep because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine Fido is walking away from his home and then suddenly stops to take a nap. The negative-sloping section of the graph represents Fido's movement away from his home, not his rest. Just like when we walk away from a starting point, the distance increases, and when we walk back, the distance decreases.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I think I get it a bit better now! So, when the line goes down, it means Fido is getting closer to home, right? But what if he just stops and doesn’t move at all? Would that be the flat part of the graph?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine Fido is standing still, not moving at all, maybe enjoying the view. Just like when we're standing in one spot, the distance from our starting point doesn't change. So, the flat part of the graph represents Fido staying in the same place, not moving closer or farther from home.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher directly addresses the rest/movement confusion with accurate explanations, but primarily tells rather than elicits reasoning, though the student does demonstrate clear improvement by correctly identifying both the negative slope (movement toward home) and flat section (rest) by Turn 2.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently grounds every explanation in concrete, relatable real-world scenarios (walking away from home, taking a nap, standing still enjoying the view) to help the student understand the abstract graph concepts.
